newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia, New Zealand "riding out" coffee rally.
newsitem.headline: Australia, New Zealand "riding out" coffee rally.

text.p: Australian and New Zealand coffee firms are riding out a 50 percent surge in international prices in the past two months, but said on Wednesday they may have to pass on the increases to consumers if the rally continues.
"The trade will ride it out until stocks diminish," said John Burton, principle of John Burton Ltd, which imports up to half of New Zealand's coffee.
He said 70 percent of the local market was in soluble coffee (instant) and beans made up a smaller proportion of the final costs in such products.
Burton blamed speculators for the rise and said supply and demand was largely in balance.

Coffee futures markets have soared in recent weeks following a smaller than expected official forecast for Brazil's crop this year, which compounded concerns over very low stocks in the United States and a period of labour unrest in Colombia which has disrupted that country's exports.
New Zealand imports a third of its coffee from Papua New Guinea, and most of the rest from Kenya and Colombia.
A far more severe price hike in wholesale prices in 1995 had only a mild impact on New Zealand retail prices, partly because of the strength of the New Zealand dollar.
Coffee roaster, distributor and retailer Andrew Ellis of Cafe L'Affare does not expect to raise prices for some time.

Ellis said he expected to wait at least three months before reviewing prices. He said the 1995 price hike caused retail prices to rise by up to 30 percent but his company was aware of consumer resistance to such increases.

A spokesman for the Australian Tea and Coffee Traders Association said Australian coffee prices had not risen so far, but it would not be long before they would be increased if international market prices did not fall.

Australian coffee roasters and wholesalers have faced a more than 50 percent increase in New York coffee futures prices in the past two months to 157 US cents a lb now from 103 cents in mid-December, the spokesman added.

But Australian retail coffee prices have not increased because local coffee sellers hold stocks of six to eight weeks. This made it unrealistic for them to vary prices in response to daily movemements in international prices, he said.
Individual coffee roasters and wholesalers contacted by Reuters also said they had not increased prices.

Australian retail coffee prices had in fact fallen slightly over the past month because of a January price decrease by the dominant coffee seller, Switzerland's Nestle, the association spokesman said.
Local coffee companies would look at a price rise in April, he said. But if the international price "dropped out of bed" there would be no price increase in Australia.

Nestle holds 70 percent of Australia's instant coffee market and has 54 percent of the country's total coffee market, by volume. The company's overall share of the Australian coffee market by value is 45 percent.
